title: Know your rights: the first five amendments
excerpt: A starting point for understanding the first five amendments to the U.S. Constitution.
author: Shari Explains
coverAlt: Original cover artwork for Know your rights: the first five amendments
body:
## The First Amendment

“Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof; or abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press; or the right of the people peaceably to assemble, and to petition the Government for a redress of grievances.”

The First Amendment states that every citizen in the United States has the right to: speak freely, petition their government, practice their own religion, and assemble.

This amendment protects YOUR right to do these things; Congress is not allowed to pass any law that violates these protected rights. The First Amendment allows you to express your grievances against the government without fear of persecution.

In today’s digital age, there is discourse about whether recording someone falls under the First Amendment. The consensus is that recording someone in public for documentation is allowed; however, you are NOT allowed to film on private property if the owner does not give you consent.

## The Second Amendment

A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State, the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed.

The Second Amendment states that anyone has the right to keep and bear arms (guns) for self-defense and/or to maintain a militia (that is, ONLY when the government calls upon citizens for protection).

This amendment protects the right to bear arms. However, there are certain rules and regulations governing the Second Amendment, as exemplified by the 1968 Gun Control Act. This law regulates the firearms industry and the possession of firearms. The law prohibits interstate firearm transfers except for manufacturers and individuals with the proper licensing.

This amendment is highly controversial; however, there’s important historical context to the Second Amendment. When the Constitution was being written, the framers feared the rise of another tyrannical rule in America. During the Revolution, the formation of a militia (known as minutemen) was essential for the Patriots’ victory.

## The Third Amendment

No Soldier shall, in time of peace be quartered in any house, without the consent of the Owner, nor in time of war, but in a manner to be prescribed by law.

In simple terms, the Third Amendment forbids the forcible housing of any soldier or military personnel, no matter the situation. The amendment requires Congress to “prescribe [it into] law” in times of war.

This amendment protects you in times of war by forbidding the Military from forcibly occupying your home. This amendment is largely seen as a relic of its time, but its historical significance is important.

When the Bill of Rights was drafted, the memory of the Crown’s rule was still prevalent in the minds of the framers. The Quartering Act of 1765 mandated that colonists allow British Soldiers to live inside their homes while they were stationed in the colonies. This act was a direct reaction to the colonists protesting British rule after the French and Indian War.

## The Fourth Amendment

The right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures, shall not be violated, and no Warrants shall issue, but upon probable cause, supported by Oath or affirmation, and particularly describing the place to be searched, and the persons or things to be seized.

The Fourth Amendment states that no law enforcement official has the right to conduct a search and seizure without obtaining a warrant that is authorized by a judge.

This amendment protects you from the police (or other government agencies) from conducting an unlawful search, which could lead to wrongful incrimination and detainment.

This amendment can also apply to people. If an officer witnesses and deems an individual’s activity as “unusual,” they have the right to stop and question the individual, but they DO NOT have the right to stop and search and/or seize any of the individual’s property.

## The Fifth Amendment

No person shall be held to answer for a capital, or otherwise infamous crime, unless on a presentment or indictment of a Grand Jury, except in cases arising in the land or naval forces, or in the Militia, when in actual service in time of War or public danger; nor shall any person be subject for the same offence to be twice put in jeopardy of life or limb; nor shall be compelled in any criminal case to be a witness against himself, nor be deprived of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law; nor shall private property be taken for public use, without just compensation.

The Fifth Amendment guarantees the right to a fair trial by a grand jury. This amendment also states that an individual will never be tried for the same crime twice; they are allowed to remain silent if they fear self-incrimination; and that the government must pay them back if their property is confiscated for public use.

This amendment protects you from a multitude of things, but the most famous example of the Fifth Amendment is “pleading the Fifth” and your Miranda rights. Pleading the Fifth and Miranda Rights technically go hand in hand, as the right to remain silent is stated in the case.

The eminent domain clause is often overlooked in terms of the Fifth Amendment. The government is required to compensate an individual if their land is seized for public use (roads, wells, schools, etc.). The compensation must equal the market value of the property taken.
